utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stein.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, my name is Bob Stein, and I represent Dario Kordic. Although we speak the same language, we are going to have to do it much slower than we normally do. Is that all right with you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I understand, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: If there is any question I ask that you don't understand, please let me know.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Perhaps you can help us by finding out those areas in which you actually can help us and those in which you cannot. Let me first start by asking, you are not a political scientist?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's correct. I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And you are not a political theorist?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I am not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You are not a journalist?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I occasionally write journalistic pieces, but I am not a full-time journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You are not a member of the working press, as it were?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, not a member of the permanent, full-time working press.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You are not a constitutional lawyer?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I am not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Or a constitutional scholar?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: In fact, you are not a college professor, currently, are you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You are not an assistant or an associate professor either?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You are not an instructor at a university?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You have no academic position currently at the University of Michigan?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I am a research associate at the Centre for Russian and East European Studies, which is an appointment that means I consult from time to time with them and lecture occasionally at various activities there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You are not paid by the University of Michigan to teach students, are you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Indeed, your position is a research position as opposed to an academic position?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: As such, of course, you are not a tenured member of the Michigan faculty?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I gather you visit Michigan two or three times a year?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Six, eight times a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. From your home in Houston?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: San Diego, California.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: San Diego, California. I'm sorry. I misspoke. The majority of your working life, you worked for Merrill Lynch?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That would be between 1981 and 1998?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: August of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And that was full-time employment?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: "Full time" in every sense of the word?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Do I take it that after 1981, in the glut of Ph.D.s, if you will, you left academia to work for Merrill?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Because you basically couldn't find a job teaching?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I had several jobs and a couple of job opportunities that I declined, but essentially you're correct. The job market wasn't such that it enabled me to find the kind of position that I wanted, so I left academia and went to work for Merrill Lynch.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: For Merrill, you were a senior resident, vice-president, and you had managerial responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And those management responsibilities were over financial consultants; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: In San Diego?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: In Fort Worth, West Texas, and in San Diego.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. During that period of time, your full-time employment was focused on your responsibilities for the brokerage house, Merrill Lynch?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, the opinion in your report, which has been forwarded to all of us, has not been put out to the general public for academic or scholarly review, has it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: It has not been peer reviewed at all?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: At all, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Before writing your report, is it fair to say that you never spoke with Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And you never spoke, obviously, at least while he was alive, to Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Or Mr. Kostroman?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Or Dr. Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's correct also.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Did you ever read the pre-trial submissions by Dario Kordic in this case?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Is it fair to say, therefore, that the primary sources of the history, the current history you're talking about were never specifically interviewed by you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I did interview Stjepan Kljuic briefly at one point in 1995, but he would be the only person, I believe, I referred to in the paper that I have interviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Right. You never asked to interview Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And you never asked to interview Tudjman, Kostroman, Boban, any of those parties?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: It is also fair to say that Dario Kordic is not mentioned in your 1994 book?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, the report that has been given to the Court and to counsel doesn't appear to have a date on it. Maybe I missed it. Did I? Is there a date on your report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't believe there's a date on it, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. Then I would like to ask, when was it written?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was completed, I would say, briefly before it was submitted to the Court, perhaps in April of this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: April 1998?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: 1999, okay. That report was written after your appearance in the Blaskic case; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Did you do more research, more writing, more analysis after your appearance in Blaskic and before you wrote your report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Okay. You reviewed that report before you testified today?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I reviewed parts of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: In fact, you made some corrections to it.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I made some additions and, I'm sure, some corrections as well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. Does that report now, as it stands, give the full, complete opinion that you have in this case?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Any additions, corrections or deletions you'd like to make?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, the report, by its nature, is a summary, and so I would present it to you as a summary of my conclusions or views on a wide variety of matters and could not probably give you additions, corrections, updates without a very extensive further report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Let me rephrase it differently. To the extent that the report sets out our opinions, it doesn't have any additions, corrections or deletions that you'd like to make now, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I also note that your report has either footnotes, endnotes, or annotations. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Your Ph.D. thesis I'm sure is filled with footnotes, endnotes, and annotations?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Endnotes, bibliography, annotations. I don't think there are any footnotes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: When you write for learned journals, you're expected to put either footnotes, endnotes, or annotations in your work?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Those annotations and footnotes would give the reader the ability to determine that which is your conclusion versus that which you are borrowing from someone else.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Among other things, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Did anyone instruct you not to put footnotes or annotations in your report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That was done on your own?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I made the decision not to incorporate footnotes in the report, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: So the reader can't tell that which is your own conclusion versus that which may be someone else's?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I would say that the context makes that clear in many cases but your point is valid. Without footnotes, the sources of quotations are not known to the reader.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. Similarly, without footnotes it's difficult to tell those of which opinions are yours and those of which are opinions held by others in the historical community.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I would say that I have at least tried to make clear the distinction, in the course of writing the paper, between my own conclusions and those of others when it became appropriate to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: We can agree, and I believe, actually, that Mr. Nice asked you this, that reasonable historians reasonably disagree?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That's what the study of history is.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Among other disciplines that's exactly what it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: It's the debate by historians over historical issues over time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Who contacted you to make an appearance here at the Tribunal? Was it the Prosecution or did you contact them? How was your introduction to the Prosecution made?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: They just called you up one day at Merrill Lynch and said, "Would you like to come on board?"

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was not at Merrill Lynch at the time that I was contacted by the Prosecution and invited to appear in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Where were you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe I was in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Where in Sarajevo? I don't mean physically but what you were doing in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was just beginning some research on a project there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The project was for whom?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's a book I'm writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That is a book in progress?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And you're writing at the library in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I'll probably write it in San Diego but the research will be done in a variety of archival institutions in South-east Europe and probably a variety of other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Did the Prosecution let you know how they got your name?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, they -- yes. They had my name from the Blaskic matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. I guess I'm going back before the Blaskic matter. How did you get hired on for the Blaskic matter?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was contacted by a member of the Prosecution team in Blaskic and invited to appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Did you ask how they got your name?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: What was the response?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was referred to them by a senior historian in the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And that would be?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: That was Denison Rusinow.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: From what school?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: He is at the university of Pittsburgh.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You and Professor Rusinow are colleagues in some fashion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That would be how?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, we've known one another since 1965, when I was first in Yugoslavia and he was living in Zagreb. So at the very beginning of my academic career and somewhere early in his academic career we got to know one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to turn our attentions now to your book and your dissertation. Can we agree that your field of concentration is not 1991 to 1994?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I think early in my career my field of concentration was the Austro-Hungarian period, and over time it has broadened as I've done additional work throughout the Twentieth Century, including the more recent period.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Your Ph.D. dissertation dealt with Bosnia and the Muslims of Bosnia-Herzegovina between 1878 and 1906?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The subject of your doctoral dissertation were the Muslims in transition; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That subject was bounded by temporal limits?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And that study dealt almost exclusively with elite Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Then, I gather, your dissertation was kind of dusted off, if you will, in 1981 and published under the title "Islam Under the Double Eagles, the Muslims of Bosnia-Herzegovina, 1878 to 1914".

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'd prefer the concept of polishing it up rather than dusting it off --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: -- and extended it somewhat in time and in topic to perhaps make it a more publishable volume.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Sure. It was extended essentially by six years or so?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. That book as well, when it was finally polished, focused on Muslims in the so-called elite period or the elite Muslims, I should say.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, your second book was with Dr. Fine and that's entitled "Bosnia, A Tradition Betrayed", and that was published in 1994?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Dr. Fine, as I gather, was your mentor at the University of Michigan?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And he's still there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: He's still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That book was written while you were employed at Merrill full time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I guess, for the purpose of the record, that's Merrill Lynch, Pierce, Fenner, Klein somebody?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Merrill Lynch is the name of the firm.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You were responsible, in that work, for anything after 1878; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And Dr. Fine took the prior history?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You didn't take a leave of absence from Merrill to work on that project?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That 1994 book relies principally on secondary sources as opposed to primary sources?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would say except insofar as both his research and mine had previously delved into primary sources it relied exclusively on secondary sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: So it's fair to say the majority of the work relies on secondary sources?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Just so we're all clear, secondary sources versus primary sources is defined how?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Secondary sources are reports of others on the basis of primary documents or findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that your 1994 book was written primarily for a popular audience as opposed to a scholarly audience?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And you don't claim that it's a scholarly work?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would say it has scholarly merit. It was not designed to be a monographic work purely for a scholarly audience.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Fair enough. Is it fair to say that up until 1994 and the publication of your second book plus one other in the field, there really did not exist, in any language, a single comprehensive history of Bosnia from the arrival of the Slavs in the Balkan Peninsula until the 1990s?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: So there was a gap in the literature which you tried to fill?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Plus, I suppose, try to make a few dollars as well?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: If that was an objective, it hasn't succeeded very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Well, we all bought some of your books.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You're welcome. Now, in 1994 -- your 1994 book, is it fair to say, was not annotated to any significant degree?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. It had footnotes but it was not annotated in the manner of scholarly monograph, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Your book focused, again, on urban Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't say that was the case. It dealt with urban/rural conflict among other things but certainly attempted to provide a synthetic history of Bosnia and Herzegovina over many centuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. The majority of your work, however, focuses on urban Bosnia, would you agree?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And your own experience living in Bosnia-Herzegovina is and was primarily an urban experience?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, I take it you also show on your resume a piece that you wrote in 1978, with an anthropologist named William Lockwood called "The Bosnian Muslims Class, Ethnicity, and Political Behaviour in a European State". You were the co-author of that piece?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: In that piece, and I quote from it: "Villages are most commonly ethnically homogenous although some villages are mixed. In the latter case, ethnic groups are usually segregated into district neighbourhoods or hamlets." Now, that's an observation that you made in that work; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That is an observation that you still believe; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. It was an observation that was valid as of the time that it was written.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Fair enough. Do you find that valid today?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Much less frequently so in contemporary Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: When from '78 to 1999 did the transition occur?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: After 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. Now, with respect to the subject of ethnic groups, you said in the same piece: "They tend to concentrate" -- Let me start again. "They tend to constitute distinct social systems superimposed on the same geographic region. Contact is limited primarily to the economic sector, especially among peasants, and this is reflected in marriage patterns, visiting patterns, communication networks, and world views." Do you agree with that statement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Then in 1995 you published a work called the "Habsburg Imperial Army in the Occupation of Bosnia-Herzegovina." It was published in a publication called "Insurrections, Wars, and the Eastern Crisis in 1870s." I gather your part of that work was pages 375 to 391?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I believe it was 1986 or '87 that that was published.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. I stand corrected. Now, in that work you call Bosnia, "Those volatile Balkan provinces." That's a quote from page 375. Do you remember using that term?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You pointed out that the Austro-Hungarian military organisations: "Contributed to the imbroglio of ethnic and social conflict in the occupied lands." Then you went on to say that: "While they," the Austrians: "Disarmed most groups and persons with violent intent and ensured that large-scale violence was no longer a viable means for Bosnians to achieve political aims, in doing so they often aroused the antagonisms of the local populations. Thus, much contention was merely rechanneled than eliminated and many of the issues came to be fought out in the political arena rather than by paramilitary forces." That's a quote from page 375. Is that an opinion you still abide by?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You went on then to say: "When Ottoman administration began to weaken in the 17th and 18th centuries, strife between the three major ethnic groups intensified." Again, something you agree with?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: "Muslim landlords frequently abused their peasants and local pashas arbitrarily taxed the population. Peasants uprisings increased and were frequently occasions of interethnic acrimony." Again, something with which you agree?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would probably today date that a little bit later than I did in that essay and say that that phenomenon started principally in the 18th century.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: In fact, you anticipated my next question because you say, and this is at page 377 of the same work: "The unrest of 1875 to 1878 exacerbated the tendencies of all ethnic groups in Bosnia and Herzegovina to organise armed bands. Serbs and Muslims had the largest paramilitary groups. Deserters from regular Ottoman army units, predominantly Bosnian Muslims, wandered the countryside looting and plundering." Agreed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that was in reference to the period after 1875 or perhaps even 1878 itself. I would have to look again. I would stand by the statement for that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: So the only issue is the period of time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. Then you went on to point out about the gendarmes, is what I would call them. How would you call them?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's good.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: By the Austrians, and you pointed out that "Most native recruits came from the lower classes, including many former surfs and urban vagabonds who had grievances against Muslim landlords. Some of the new recruits used their newly acquired status and weapons to intimidate their former oppressors. Muslim landlords found it particularly galling to be abused by --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down because of the translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: " -- and religiously inferior. The gendarmes thus --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: "The gendarmes thus often contributed to ethnic and social conflict rather than reducing it." Again, an opinion you still agree with?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: We're almost done our little trip through your works, but let me just ask a couple of things before I move on. You noted between 1878 and 1881 that Serbian brigans terrorised Muslim landlords; is that a correct statement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: It would be correct well into 1882.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Consequently, I gather, "the gendarmes functioned after 1883 mainly to," I can't read my own handwriting here, essentially to vitiate against collisions between the rival ethnic groups. That's a paraphrase, not a direct quote.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that the gendarmes came about after 1883 to try to deal with this situation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, the gendarmes entered the picture in order to establish order and Austro-Hungarian rule following the peasant rebellion of 1881/1882, and that role was really a dual one. It was both to establish taxation authority and, generally, state authority, and it was to end the conflict between peasants and landlords.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And that conflict was a rival conflict between rival ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was a conflict between Serbian peasants and Muslim landlords and was ethnic in character, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Then moving forward, you note: "By the early 20th century, the interest of Bosnian ethnic groups were represented not by brigan bands but by ethnic political leaders who presented their extensive demands to high imperial authorities." Still a true statement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, let's fast-forward to 1994 in your book, and let me just give you a caption from that book that I think capsulates what you're trying to say and ask you if you still stand by it. "Some observers have portrayed the Bosnian conflict as a renewal of age-old mutual hatreds that inexorably resurfaced after the collapse of Tito's communist regime. In contrast, we assert that the current Bosnian crisis is, in the context of Bosnian history, an historical apparition, albeit with a single important historical precedent, the interethnic slaughter of the World War II era. Armed conflict, ethnic cleansing, the bombardment of cities, and atrocities against civilians in Bosnia were not preordained consequences of ethnonational divisions in Bosnian society. They developed as a result of the transformation of the YPA into an instrument of Serbian nationalists, the annexationist ambitions of the Croatian and Serbian governments, and the eagerness of national extremists to conduct unsavoury ethnic cleansing campaigns with the endorsement and assistance of organised armies in that region." Does that capsulise your position?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That book, in fact, "Bosnia-Herzegovina, a Tradition Betrayed," has been criticised for "overemphasising perhaps the degree of harmony between the nations generally." Fair enough?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Among other things, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I actually have one here just to make sure you know we bought it.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: In fact, your book was reviewed, when it came out, by a variety of folks. One such review, Mr. Kislinger, from the New Leader, wrote in September of '94: "Donia and Fine's view of Bosnia culture is, on the whole, compelling, but its presentation is troubling. Having defined Bosnian tradition as free from interethnic strife, they must engage in contortions to explain the region's long record of bloodshed, including peasant revolts under the Ottomans and local nationalists, especially Serbian resistance to Habsburg rule, Yugoslav and Titoist rule. All of these have ethnic and religious --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Kindly slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I will try again. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may help the witness and the other people taking notes if there are other copies of the book that can be made available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: At the moment, I think that is going to take up more time. Can you remember in these quotations, Mr. Stein, to go as slowly as possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I'll try, sir. We always have the yin/yang of going slow, but move fast, and I will try my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Picking up: "All of these have ethnic and religious aspects. When such purported aberrations are attributed solely to class differences or outside forces, the argument begins to sound circular. Bosnia is tolerant, and if it sometimes hasn't been, it was not acting like Bosnia. By focusing on urban culture as the true picture of Bosnia, the authors neglect the more refractory countryside where, in fact, much of the current conflict is rooted. "Finally, the atrocities of World War II constitute an exception so drastic it virtually disproves the rule." You've read that before, obviously?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Essentially, at least Kislinger was critiquing your work as overly optimistic; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't hear the word "optimistic" there. I wouldn't characterise the book as overly optimistic. Maybe I missed it but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. He certainly was making some critiques on the distinction between urban and rural life?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Similarly, Mr. Robert Kingvold, in a book review on foreign affairs, makes a similar kind of observation about your book, does he not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I've only seen one review in foreign affairs, and you'll have to refresh my memory. I don't recall anything negative in it but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. He called it "something of the character of a skilled high school text." Not very favourable.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I think if you read the last sentence of that review, you would find it very favourable.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: In the Times literary supplement, Charles Kinna went on to say: "The author's treatment of Bosnian history is somewhat facile. The style often borders on invective, and from cover to conclusion, the notion of a tradition betrayed buzzes annoyingly along the surface of the narrative. The book's project is to show that the current Bosnian government, in opposing the territorial division of the republic into ethnically based states, represents a 'tradition of tolerance and coexistence that goes many centuries.' To anyone familiar with the history of the Balkans, the picture that emerges will appear rather rosy." Now, there are other criticisms and critiques of your works besides these, are there not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You acknowledge, sir, that there are historians and experts in the Balkan regions who claim that Balkan hatred existed long before any manipulation of Balkan leaders?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I would probably be one of them. I did not make the case then and I would not make it now that there were no hatreds in the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Can we further agree that reports of long-time neighbours raping, murdering, and expelling their neighbours suggest that old hatreds lie so close to the surface that it would not take much to bring them out into the open?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can't agree with that statement unless it's bounded in time in terms of what sorts of hatreds or animosities might be there. I would want to, I think, qualify that somewhat in terms of time frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Let's take 1991 to 1994.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe the statement that you read suggested some age-old animosities, and my question would be how old.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Certainly, as presented by the Prosecution, you agreed, and I believe you said the secretary of state, U.S. Secretary of State James Baker in the early '90s and others took the long-standing view that there were ethnic hatreds in the Balkans?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Secretary of State Christopher, in March of 1993, took the position that these people had been killing each other for centuries as a way of announcing the new American hands-off policy towards Bosnia. He took that position consistently thereafter during his tenure as secretary of state, at least until the eve of the Dayton discussions. Yes, that was closely allied with the policy preference of the U.S. government at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Indeed, just to wrap this section up, we can agree that there's no consensus on the issue of ethnic hatreds in the dozens of books and articles published in the last few years?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: We could agree on that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Journalists travelling amongst the region tend to emphasise the deep-seated nature of the hatreds, while books focusing on politics and history tend to emphasise the responsibility of the leaders; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: As a very broad generalisation, yes, but I can think of many exceptions to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: No question about it, going back to our reasonable historians can reasonably disagree.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would say that the generalisation for journalists is no longer valid in terms of recent works that have appeared by journalists who have spent substantial time in the region.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. I want to turn very briefly to your time in the region. Do I take it you have professional colleagues currently in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And friends in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Do I take it that many of those friends and professional colleagues are Muslims or Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Few are Croats?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Some are Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: But certainly the minority?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: There's no majority. I would say that many of them are, probably not a majority, but the plurality of them are Bosniaks. Some are Serbs. Some are Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All living around the Sarajevo area?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Do I take it in 1994, the fall, you began discussions with Inis Kujundzic, and I'm sure I've mispronounced that name, K-U-J-U-N-D-Z-I-C --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Kujundzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: -- who's the director of the national and university library in Sarajevo, to help rebuild the library holdings?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I had discussions with him, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Of course, the library had been destroyed in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: In August of 1992, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Do I take it you, in March of 1995, delivered a bibliography, along with Dr. Fine, and gave some lectures in Sarajevo on the content of your works?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You are currently working on a web page with a University of Sarajevo professor?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I am not actively working on that project right now. I'm aware of it and was involved very early on in establishing it but am not actively involved at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Your visit in 1994 was part of a mobile university sponsored by the National Peace Foundation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: What is the National Peace Foundation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm really not certain what -- I don't know very much about it at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Was that a paid visit or did they pay your expenses?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: They arranged transportation into -- from Zagreb into Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And that visit was also part of the Sarajevo-based FAMA, the F-A-M-A foundation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: What is FAMA?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is a word that stands for nothing. It is a foundation that was established to facilitate the visit of various people to Bosnia-Herzegovina by a small group of people who support artistic and scholarly work.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Do you know where the financial support and funds come for these --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Stein, we haven't really got all the time in the world to go through this sort of detail. Move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I'm going to skip over something and move right along here. I'd like to talk to you about a few historical watersheds, if I may. First, the gathering at Gazimestan, can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: This was a huge rally sponsored by President Slobodan Milosevic on the 500th anniversary of the battle of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And its significance?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was the major event in the, let's say, transformation of the government of Serbia from being a republic, which was committed to the ideals of the socialist era, to a nationalist government.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Those pieces of information you gathered after your testimony in the Blaskic case; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: So you did some further research on the issues?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm always doing research on such issues and gather information, both by coincidence and by design, so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You were specifically asked about Gazimestan in Blaskic and didn't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said I didn't know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Can you tell us also about the significance of the miner's strike in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would only be speculating if I addressed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. Can you tell us if you know the name Miroslav Solijevic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Doctor, I want you to focus your attention, please, on life in the country of Yugoslavia under the communist system. Would you agree that Marshal Tito ruthlessly suppressed any expression of resurgent nationalism? He enforced his doctrine of brotherhood and unity and carried out purges of Serbs, Croats, Muslims, Slovenes, Macedonians, and Albanians, balancing his repression of one nation against that of another?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Would you further agree that nationalists were forced into exile where they nurtured their resentment in expatriate communities which proved fertile breeding grounds for nationalism or they were gaoled?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And would you further agree that: "Bosnia acquired a reputation for labouring under the most repressive of all the communist regimes in Yugoslavia? The authorities clamped down on each of Bosnia's three communities. A Muslim trial would often be followed by a case involving a Serb or a Croat. "more than anywhere else in Yugoslavia the doctrine of brotherhood and unity was rigidly enforced in Bosnia-Herzegovina." Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: The first one, if it pertained to Yugoslavia as a whole, one would want to limit that assertion to the early years of socialism. So I'm not quite following, I'm afraid, your extensive quotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Actually, I'm quoting from a book, "The Death of Yugoslavia", by Laura Silber and Alan Little. Are you familiar with this book?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: It is a recognised work on the area -- in the area?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Well thought of and well regarded?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: By most, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: They note, at page 228 of the book, all that I said. Let's break it down in its pieces. "Bosnia had required a reputation for labouring under the most repressive of all communist regimes in Yugoslavia." Agreed, disagreed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's the statement that I would specify would particularly pertain to the early years. I think that Bosnia actually went through several different phases. At times it probably was far behind a couple of its neighbours anyway, and then in the 1980s it became very repressive of nationalist excesses, deviations as they were called in that time, and then totally lost that character at the end of the 1980s.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Ms. Silber and Mr. Little say that: "After Tito's death and the ensuing political crises, the number of political trials increased and the wounded Bosnian regime tried to sustain itself through repression." Agree, disagree?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with that statement as it stands. I think that the Bosnian regime, up until the late 1980s, was probably one of the most confident and certainly the most loyal to Titoist ideals. So I wouldn't describe it as wounded. In fact, it had substantial links with the, let's say, federal institutions and in some sense it benefited from their support.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Doctor, are you aware that in July and August of 1983, 13 Bosnian Muslims were tried in a Sarajevo District Court, accused conspiring to transform Bosnia into an Gazimestan?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe you can find that in "Bosnia and Herzegovina, Tradition Betrayed", and yes, I am aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Were you further aware that there's actually a part of the Criminal Code whose aim was to protect the idea of brotherhood and unity, that would be Article 134 of the Yugoslavia Criminal Code that is translated to read: "Incitement of national, racial, religious hatred and intolerance. "(1) Who, through propaganda or in any other way incites or provokes national, racial, or religious hatred, or infraction among nations and national minorities that live within Yugoslavia shall be punished with one to ten years of imprisonment." Are you aware that was the law?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: As you noted, I'm not a constitutional scholar. I am aware that there was legislation that permitted both republican organs and Central Yugoslavia organs to prosecute national excesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to know if we can agree on this, and that is that: "The configuration of national and ethnic conflict which emerged during the period of disintegration, and we're talking about disintegration of Tito's republic, was intimately tied up with the policies of communism. Communism was as much a part of the problem as the solution to the problem of intercommunal conflict in the region." Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: You're asking me to agree to a very broad general statement by someone else who has tried to put it together, and I would not construe it that way. I don't fully disagree with the statement but couldn't adopt it as my own view of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. That statement is from Dr. Allcock's report. He will be a witness in this case later. He also says: "Efforts were made to promote a common Yugoslav identity. This was based upon the picture of peoples united in a common struggle against fascism in brotherhood and unity." You'd agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would agree with it for the early period, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You would disagree later on in the Tito period?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would not agree with it for the period after roughly the late 1960s.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Let me just raise this with you, Doctor, according to Dr. Allcock: "The communist government engaged in periodic campaigns against national chauvinism with well-published prosecutions of those accused of fostering intercommunal antagonism. These occasional campaigns had the unwitting effect in certain celebrated cases of making the objects of state attention into future martyrs to the national cause available to be employed as potent symbols of continuing resistance to communist attempts to suppress the nation when Yugoslavia began to break up. Thus Franjo Tudjman and Alija Izetbegovic in Bosnia both acquired considerable political capital from their experience of imprisonment at the hands of the communist authorities." That's a large chunk, I realise, and I will give you a chance to discuss it, but do you agree in principle with those precepts?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I would add Vojislav Seselj to that list of names and would agree with the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Would you spell his name, sir, for the translators?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: S-e-s-e-l-j as -- maybe someone can provide a better Slavic language --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Very good, sir. Your report, in fact, notes that Yugoslavia was held together by two key institutions, the League of Communists and the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You go on to note -- I am sorry, I said your book. I meant your report. You go on to say in your report that according to the 1994 constitution, the JNA was to uphold the socialist order and ensure the unity of Yugoslavia as a country.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think I specify 1974 constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Did I say '84?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: You said '94.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Are you aware of the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: What is that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: The Academy of Sciences existed in each of the six republics of the former Yugoslavia and promoted to the level or title of academic were those people who were distinguished scholars in the view of the existing members of the academy, so the academies functioned both in a sense of meeting places of the leading intellectuals of the time and also occasionally they facilitated publication and certain types of scholarly work.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: This was in each of the republics?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: In each of the republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Were the findings, or the memos, or the writings, or conclusions of the various academies taken very seriously in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, the -- I don't know that they had findings. They would frequently, as I say, facilitate publication by members, and on occasion members would come together to issue some sort of a political statement or declaration, and any pronouncements of their members or groups of members were always treated with great seriousness, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: By the way, just parenthetically, Dr. Tudjman was a member of the Croatian academy, was he not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: In 1986, September of 1986, I'm given to understand that the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts essentially opined that: "Yugoslavia, in its present form, was no longer an adequate solution to the Serbian question." Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that date is wrong as well, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: When do you think the publication occurred?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think it was 1966.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think we need worry about the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's quite a well-known memorandum. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Can we agree that: "The draft memorandum did not create nationalism, it simply tapped sentiments that ran deep among the Serbs but which were repressed and as a result exacerbated by communism. The academy's tract echoed opinions whispered throughout Serbia." Perhaps a little dramatic in presentation but, nonetheless, can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: We cannot. You disagree with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Again, that is presented by Ms. Silber and Mr. Little in their book "Death of Yugoslavia." You take issue with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would not formulate the conclusion that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. How would you formulate the conclusion, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: To what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Stein, you're doing something that I'm rather familiar with. You are taking our expert through the whole literature on Yugoslavia as if you are asking him to defend his doctoral thesis, and that is not the point of the cross-examination. I think that what interests us, as members of this Trial Chamber and as professional Judges, is to cross-examine the expert Donia on what he alleges in his report. You have Mr. Donia's report. It was presented to us by the Prosecutor. Could you please limit your comments to what he himself said, because that is the objective of a cross-examination. It is not to take Dr. Donia through all the literature on ex-Yugoslavia as if we were testing his knowledge. You have already touched upon his credibility. I think it is time for us to focus on the report. Could you please do that? We have it in front of us. I know that you have a host of literature that you have brought with you, many books, but you will have the opportunity to use them, I believe, on another occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Certainly I take your point, Your Honour, and I was really trying to bring myself up to create for the Court a picture of life under the communist country, a theme we had talked about with some of the witnesses, but I will certainly move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Doctor, can you help us with one short question, and that is: In the late 1980s, as the Republic was breaking down, can you, in a very short way, describe for all of us the manner in which the Serbian government, headed by Mr. Milosevic, came to the forefront in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not too sure what you mean by "came to the forefront." The fact is that the efforts of President Milosevic to essentially transform the leadership in various republics gave Milosevic control of four of the eight members of the collective presidency, and the way in which that happened was essentially through, first of all, his taking power within the Republic of Croatia -- or, excuse me, the Republic of Serbia. He tried to take power later in the Republic of Croatia, but he took power over the position of his former mentor in Serbia, and then arranged a series of street demonstrations in the three republics that were -- or one republic that was closest to Serbia, namely Montenegro, and also in the autonomous provinces of Vojvodina and Kosovo. By using street demonstrations, which had really never been a part of the political repertoire for major decision-making under socialism, the leaderships of those areas resigned or were forced out and replaced by leaders loyal to President Milosevic. He made similar efforts to destabilise the government of Slovenia, and more subtle efforts to destabilise the government of Bosnia, and subsequently came to support the Serbian minority in the Republic of Croatia. That process is the way in which the Serbian government came to play in an inordinately important role in the Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia in its final days.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Is it fair to say also in so doing, Milosevic rode the wave of nationalism that he created?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't think that he created it. He stimulated it and supported an existing trend that had been whipped up for some time, for several years prior to that in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And used it for his own political ends?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: To enhance his power?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: To enhance his power and the role of Serbs and the Republic of Serbia within the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All this, of course, is not limited purely to Serbia. He was thinking beyond his borders, as you just indicated?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: When Milosevic was doing all that we just discussed, certainly the other republics were reacting as well?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Do I take it that you agree or disagree that the Slovenian president was the first to really come to heads with Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would say the first people to come to heads with Mr. Milosevic were the leaders of Vojvodina and Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Why would you say that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Because that -- let me just correct that and say that I think that Milosevic was at loggerheads with the leaders of virtually every republic effectively from the time that he came to power.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You mentioned again Vojvodina and Kosovo as the first targets. Why do you think they were the first targets?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: The effort that Milosevic made was to assure leadership loyal to him in republics in which he could most easily accomplish his objectives. The obvious targets were those which were constitutionally part of Serbia, that is, the autonomous provinces, and Montenegro, which was also historically sympathetic with Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. Thereafter, after those first preliminary political skirmishes, where was the focus of Milosevic's aims then?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I describe that process, I guess, as the creation of a greater Serbian coalition, and I think it would be safe to say that his aspirations lay in all areas of the former Yugoslavia, particularly those in which there was a substantial Serbian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Can we agree that Slovenia was the first republic to really break from the fold?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: As the declarations of independence of Slovenia and Croatia took place on the same day, by virtue of the armed conflict, Slovenia was the first one which broke free. But I would not necessarily see the Slovene effort as particularly ahead of the Croatian one after the elections of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. So it's your view that the republics of both Slovenia and Croatia basically launched their own existence at the same time and consequently departed from the republic at the same time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's a process, and the two, at that point, tended to move forward together. I would say this: I think the tensions between the Slovenes and the Serbs prior to the elections of 1990 would, in fact, correspond to your original premise in the question, that those were probably the worst relations in the period prior to the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Can we agree, Doctor, that in these early discussions, the issue between Serbia and Slovenia really boiled down to the acceptable level of democracy or democratisation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't concur.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Doctor, let me ask you about the different visions that there were when the republic broke down in terms of the internal organisation of Yugoslavia, so we're going to rewind a little bit. Can we agree that the Serbs wanted a centralised government whereas the Slovenes wanted the opposite?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: When you say "republic," I take it you mean the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your question was that the Serbs wanted a centralised government and the Slovenes wanted the opposite?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: By which you mean a decentralised government, a decentralised federal government?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And Serbia was confidant -- I don't mean confidant. Serbia's position was that introducing a one man, one vote would halt the forces that were tearing apart the federation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: At one point, that was the view of the Slovene leadership, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And that view was held for what reason, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: They were hoping that the federal elections at the federal level would defuse the, let's say, Serbian nationalist momentum.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That would be because why?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm not following your --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Why would the nationalist momentum be diminished?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think there were two reasons for it: Number one, I think they hoped that this would be more than simply a plebiscite in which everyone voted along ethnic lines, but the Serbs within Yugoslavia, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, did not constitute a majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: But they could outvote the Slovenes; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And the Slovenes, on the other hand, insisted on retaining a one federal unit, one vote government, which was set forth in the 1974 constitution?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I think this is grossly oversimplifying it. I'm not sure what time period you're talking about here, and perhaps it would be wise to identify the time that you're referring to. Let me ask if you can identify perhaps a time it refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: This would have been in the late '80s when the republic was still in existence and they were debating what it was going to look like post-Tito.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: So prior to the break-up or destruction, whatever, of the League of Communists?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. That generalisation would hold for that time, yes. Within the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, there were all these discussions about how to arrive at some sort of resolution that would preserve the federation, and the Slovenes tended to be extremely oriented towards a decentralised solution and the Serbs towards a central one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I'm going to jump ahead somewhat. After 1990 in Bosnia, that became the same kind of issue, with the one man, one vote issue versus the one area issue.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: What's the question? I'm not sure what --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The same kind of debate occurred in Bosnia after 1990 as to what Bosnia was to look like; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was one of many issues that was raised, but I think that once the elections were scheduled, this ceased to be, let's say, a point of contention. It was a concern to the -- let me put it this way: I think the concern of the leadership of the HDZ, the Croatian Democratic Community, after it was formed came to focus around the establishment of the community of Croats as one of three co-equal communities, and that to assure that co-equality -- they wanted to assure that equality because it was the smallest of the three national groups in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I jumped forward but I want to go back again to when the break-up of the former Yugoslavia was occurring. Can we agree that at that point in time, it was Milosevic's preference to gain control over Yugoslavia through the existing structures of the communist party and the federal government, but that option apparently slipped by his grasp? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would formulate it somewhat differently. I think the primary concern of -- again, depending on specifically the time frame, the greatest concern that Milosevic had was, in fact, the triumph of the reformist approach, and so his effort was focused on defeating this effort by the reformist group so that he ended up kind of sabotaging that initiative in order to assure that the purely nationalist perspective would prevail.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Can we agree further that, at least according to Noel Malcolm, Milosevic's second option was that if Yugoslavia could not be controlled as a single entity, he would carve out of it a new entity, an extended Serbian territory which would be his and his alone?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would just like to point out that I did not concur with your earlier statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: So I'm not agreeing further.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Would you ask the question again, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Sure. Would you agree with Noel Malcolm's observation that if Yugoslavia could not be controlled as a single entity, then Milosevic would carve out of it a new entity, an extended Serbian territory which would be his and his alone?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Can you identify the period that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: During the break-up of the republic.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: What would that be?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Any time frame that you would like to use, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would say that that statement would be broadly true and in the course of a sequence of events from -- I would find difficulty putting specific time frames around it, but certainly from somewhere in early 1991 going forward to the period of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Fine. In that time frame, you agree with the statement; is that right, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Can we agree further, there is a thing called the greater Serbian coalition?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And the greater Serbian coalition had members found in Serbia, Kosovo, Montenegro, Croatia, and Bosnia; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Of course, these populations were not contiguous with each other?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Generally, that's true. They weren't all contiguous with one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: As a result, Serbia, in some ways, had to neutralise Muslims and others in areas in which Serbs were in a minority, Croatia, Bosnia, Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Again, without a time frame that you're speaking about, I'm not sure I can stipulate to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That would be during the period 1991 to 1994.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Again, with relationship to various areas at various times, I would concur with the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Again, I think we can agree that Mr. Milosevic supported and fomented Serbian nationalists movements in all the other republics of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, except Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And that's primarily because there are very few Serbs in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No contiguous Serbian population there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Can we agree that after the 19 -- well, let me rephrase that. You're aware, of course, that in 1989 there were amendments to the Serbian constitution?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's mentioned in the paper and in the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: These were done, again, by the Serbs themselves unilaterally?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: They were done unilaterally by the Serbian government, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Serbia wanted to introduce a one man, one vote which means that the numerically superior Serbs could outvote the Slovenes? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: What period are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: After the March 1989 amendments.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: What document are you suggesting that they wanted to introduce this one man, one vote principle to?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Doctor, as a general matter, and I'm asking the question, can we agree that Serbia wanted to introduce a one man, one vote system which would mean that the numerically superior Serbs would outvote the Slovenes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Where does this appear in the report? How does it arise from the report or the witness's evidence, Mr. Stein?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The report mentions, but I don't think fully, the ambitions of Mr. Milosevic and its effect on the region, and this question lays the foundation for that. It also lays the foundation for the ultimate political debate within the republic itself, the former republic, and within Bosnia. It's all part of the period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Stein, I said yesterday that time would be limited, and I repeat that. We've got at least one other witness for this week. We will be adjourning in a few minutes when you get to a convenient moment. You should aim to finish your cross-examination this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: This is a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Before we adjourn, is Dr. Allcock here or will he be here tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He is here and available for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How long is he likely to be in chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No longer than this witness in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Cross-examination of that witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: As we mentioned the other day, we have not had full time to work with our client in the Croatian version of his report, and as a result, we had an agreement with the Prosecution by which we would do a limited exam initially, followed by the rest of our exam after we had more time to digest the report in Croatian. It was contemplated he would make two appearances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How much of his report have you managed to get through in the Croatian?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Not much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, have you much for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: For Dr. Allcock, not too much, but I would like to know -- I'm waiting for what the other Defence will define, and then I can decide whether to go broadly or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As far as this witness is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Probably fifteen minutes, half an hour maximum, I guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
