utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. We will adjourn now and sit again at ten past four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stein.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Doctor, let me just wrap up where we were before we go to another area, and that is, can we agree that in 1990, and that's the period we're talking about, it was not the goal of either Slovenia or Croatian politicians to break up the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I would not want to speculate on the motives of at least some of them. It was certainly not the stated goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I'd like to turn our attentions, please, to the meetings that took place in and around the Karadjordjevo meeting, and I'd like to give to the Court, please, a summary that we prepared relative to the meetings that were taking place in and about January of 1991 through July of 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is marked D41/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Doctor, I've tried to do this in a summary way. Would you take a look at the document? You can see the source materials at the end. When you're done looking at it, just let us know.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Doctor, having taken a look at our document now marked D41, is this a fair summary of the meetings that were going on in January, February, March, April, up to June and July '91 regarding the future of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think it's a fair and excellent summary of the meetings between the heads of the various republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Fair enough. Do I take your answer to mean there were also meetings going on below the heads-of-republic levels?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Amongst other politicians?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Amongst other politicians, between heads of republics and other politicians, including those from other republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Sure. Does your study of the period also indicate that although these were the official meetings, there were pre-meeting meetings, post-meeting meetings, phone calls, other kinds of communications?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: There certainly were, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The Karadjordjevo meeting that we were discussing yesterday and today, occurred right in the middle of that, in March of 1991, am I right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: It did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, yesterday you opined that that was the meeting at which Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Tudjman divided up Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe you'll find that I suggested that they reached an agreement in principle to pursue the division of Bosnia but reached no agreement on the territorial provisions of that division.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Indeed, your report at page 36 says that they met behind closed doors and "probably reached an agreement."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, this is a new conversion for you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I would say that I have become convinced by several interviews that I've seen in the press by Mr. Dusan Bilandzic in which he describes quite explicitly the agreement that was reached at Karadjordjevo, and then the subsequent effort to achieve a territorial agreement which failed. That interview, I think, was first done with Nacional sometime late in 1991 and was subsequently reproduced in a number of places, and in addition, I believe, he testified regarding that meeting in the Blaskic matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You, in the Blaskic matter, testified as to this meeting, that you were an agnostic as to whether or not such an agreement was reached?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You've now changed your opinion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I feel confident that given the evidence I've seen from Mr. Bilandzic that, yes, this did indeed take place, again the agreement in principle without an agreement on territorial provisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: In the Blaskic case, you indicated that you could not conclude anything other than that there was extensive speculation and you could draw no conclusion from that speculation.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think I noted that there was extensive speculation in the press immediately subsequent to that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bilandzic did not participate in these negotiations; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: He participated in the subsequent territorial discussions, according to his account.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I want to make clear that we understand that the meeting between Milosevic and Tudjman was man to man.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know that there's absolute certainty on that, but that's been the report from the people who were closest to it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Right. There's no one closer and these two men, who's ever come out and said they were in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I'd like to hand you a letter in both Croatian and English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Judge, we don't have a French version. We'll make sure that happens. I'd like to pass this around.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is marked D42/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to look -- well, when you have had a chance to consume that letter, just let me know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Stein, I think that we need a better copy. We're no longer so young, so we can't read just any copy. The visibility of this one is not very good, even in English. Even in English it is not legible. So that I am not only complaining about the fact that I only have an English version but also regarding the readability of this copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: We'll rectify, that Your Honour. I'll get a better copy. We concur with your --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Stein. The microphone is not switched on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Doctor, have you had a chance to read the letter?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I want specifically -- this is a letter dated July 5, 1992. I want to specifically focus on paragraph 3. This is, of course, Dr. Tudjman writing to Mr. Izetbegovic. "Serbian aggression in Bosnia and Herzegovina has inflicted huge suffering to both Muslim and Croatian peoples. Most of the aggressor's operations are continued to be directed at the districts where Croats constitute majority. That fact reveals the absurdity of the accusations about the conspiracy between Croatian and Serbian representatives at the expense of the Muslim people." Did you follow that, Doctor, as I was reading it, because of the blurred copy?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: My question to you is that certainly reveals, does it not, that Dr. Tudjman certainly was denying that there was an agreement to divide up Bosnia, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think Dr. Tudjman has consistently denied that there was an agreement to divide up Bosnia, and it is particularly disingenuous to have this letter, dated July 5th, which is only two days after the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna had assumed powers of sovereignty over its territory and, one, the universal condemnation of the United States State Department, the world press, and the various leadership groups within Sarajevo, and the members of the Croatian Community or the HDZ who were opposed to this partition policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Doctor, we can agree, can we not, that Croatia was the first country to recognise the independence of BiH?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And Croatia was the first to send an Ambassador to BiH?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now just posit this, Doctor, if you will, people change their minds do, they not, and isn't it conceivable that even if there was the kind of discussion that you have now converted to believing between Tudjman and Milosevic, that given the nature of what happened thereafter, Tudjman changed his mind?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I think probably the most compelling evidence of the likelihood of an agreement at Karadjordjevo in fact comes from behaviour, the behaviour of the HVO, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and the HDZ as it fell under the control of those forces who favoured separatism from Bosnia. So is it possible that he changed his mind? Yes. Is there evidence that he ever did? I haven't seen any evidence that would suggest that he changed his mind on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: How about evidence of the fact that in 1992, President Tudjman accepted the internationally agreed upon boundaries of BiH?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think there are many instances of this nominal recognition and verbal acceptance, and accompanying denials of any agreement at Karadjordjevo or anywhere else on the part of President Tudjman. One can find no shortage of declarations, pronouncements, and statements such as this. The record is replete with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: So on the one hand you're positing influence and innuendo gained through newspaper accounts, and on the other hand we have the actions of recognising Bosnia, of sending an ambassador, of recognising their international borders, yet you draw the conclusion that he participated in a division of Bosnia in 1991?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: The behaviour to which I refer is the behaviour of actual organisations, military and civilian, that carried out the intended partition. I recognise your point, that there are numerous other pronouncements and declarations, and as I have indicated, I think that it's hard to find a press conference that President Tudjman had in this period in which he didn't deny that there was such an agreement or such an intent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Certainly on the issue of whether or not there was such an agreement, that's again one of these things that historians can reasonably disagree on?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think the record on the question of an agreement in principle at Karadjordjevo is now overwhelmingly in favour of the idea that there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Overwhelmingly means there is a minority view as well.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. There's always a minority view.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And Mr. Milosevic, the other party to the agreement, has also spoken about whether there was one; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: He basically said, and I'm going to quote from him, if I may: "Tudjman told me he wanted an independent Croatia but we simply could not agree. He wanted to destroy the federal institutions and I could not agree to that. I suggested, as I had before, that we should change the constitution to allow self-determination. "There has been speculation that we decided how to split Yugoslavia. I can tell you now that if we had decided that there, we could have done it immediately. I believe the best solution for all was to live in one country." He's quoted in Ms. Silber and Mr. Little's book and that's the quote. Do you take him at his word for that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Let's again look at actions. The next day after this purported agreement, the Serbs attacked and took over a police station, correct, in Plitvice?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I couldn't, just independently sitting here, confirm that. I will just take your word for it that that was the date of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: In August '91, Vukovar, which was a Croatian city, was completely destroyed by the Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would say that was a later date. It was utterly destroyed in the latter months of 1991, culminating in the abandonment of the city by the Croatian forces. I believe it was November 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: When did the destruction start?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Oh, it started August, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: August of '91?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Right after this agreement supposedly?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, that's a ways after the agreement but, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. Then Dubrovnik was destroyed as well?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, Dubrovnik was not destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: When was the attack on Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were several attacks on Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The first?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sometime in the August/September time frame.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: After this purported agreement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, again, regardless of what was said or not said between the parties, there began conflict, real armed conflict in the summer of 1991 between Serbs and Croats?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: In October of '91 there was a peace conference right in this very city, correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. The conference on Yugoslavia was convened here in The Hague and was in more or less continuous or ongoing session for some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Dr. Tudjman was present?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: At some of them he was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: At that peace conference he agreed with others there would be no unilateral change of borders, did he not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Indeed, ultimately the Vance-Owen Plan -- let me rephrase that. When the Vance-Owen Plan finally came out, Bosnia was recognised within the existing borders that had existed in 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you, if we can, to turn to page 34 of your report, for those of you who have the report.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I, unwisely, do not, Mr. Stein.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Maybe we can put a copy of it up on the ELMO. Just the one page would be fine. You quote, at page 34 of your report, Warren Zimmerman. Do you see the quote that's listed in your report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You say, and the quote speaks for itself, so I won't repeat it for everyone, but, again, you use this as evidence of Dr. Tudjman's positions; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Among other things. I quoted this citation from Mr. Zimmerman because it spells out somewhat President Tudjman's thinking on why he believes that Bosnia should be a part of Croatia. As I indicated yesterday, there was a much more extensive session on the 14th of January, 1992 in which Ambassador Zimmerman was regaled for about an hour about the fact that Bosnia ought to be part of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Let's just stick with this quote. The first sentence is important: "Unlike Milosevic, who is driven by power, Tudjman betrayed an obsession with creating nationalism." That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you, if we can, to take a look at the actual work that you're quoting from itself, Warren Zimmerman's book, and while it's being passed around, we just have the cover page, Warren Zimmerman was whom?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Warren Zimmerman was the last U.S. ambassador to Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D43/1.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Is there a copy for the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The interpreters have asked for a copy, and there certainly is an extra one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Would you put the Zimmerman pages in front of you, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: In fact, having taken a look at it now, you've transposed two pages from Zimmerman's book, have you not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I've done it in the normal fashion of taking two sentences and separating them by the three periods.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The first sentence of Zimmerman's book has a word difference that I think is important. Let's start first with the paragraph that is on page 75: "Unlike Milosevic, who was driven by power, Tudjman betrayed an obsession with Croatian nationalism. His devotion to Croatia was of the most narrow-minded sort." Right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You must have made a typographical error there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Indeed, if the paragraphs are read as the book flows, can we agree that there is a little different meaning?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would certainly agree that the section we just read from would -- I mean, I think it's, indeed, the case that President Tudjman is not obsessed with creating nationalism. So this rendition of it is a welcomed correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: At page 74, Zimmerman notes: "The most troubling part of our conversation concerned Bosnia. Tudjman stated flatly, and with no evidence, Bosnia has historically been a part of Croatia and has always been in Croatia's geopolitical sphere. Not only do Croats live in Bosnia, but most Muslims in Bosnia consider themselves Croats." Right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, having read these in context, can't we conclude that the discussion, as referenced in Zimmerman's book, dealt with Croatia proper, the nation of Croatia proper, let me finish the thought, and had no specific application or reference to his attitude towards Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I am not following that line of reasoning here. I would see your point in the second -- on the page 75 quote in his statement that his devotion to Croatia was of the most narrow-minded sort. That pertains to Croatia. The statement on page 74, it seems to me, is pertaining to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The two need to be read together, don't you think, Doctor, in due fairness?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I put them together and probably omitted the intervening sentence or two there and would say that the first paragraph here, in which Ambassador Zimmerman finds himself very troubled by these assertions that Bosnia has historically been a part of Croatia, pertains to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. We will let the reader make his own judgement. You and I can agree that Dr. Tudjman never advocated in his book or anywhere else a violent overthrow or changes in the borders?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: We can further agree that Dr. Tudjman does not, in his works, underline or show or disseminate any nationalistic -- let me rephrase that. Dr. Tudjman, in his works, does not reveal any nationalistic hatred towards any nation, and specifically towards Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm afraid you and I could not agree on that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you your testimony in the Blaskic case. You were asked: "Q Tudjman, in that work, does he anywhere underline or disseminate nationalistic hatred towards any nation, and specifically towards the Bosniaks?" And your answer was no.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'd have to be refreshed on what work we're speaking of. I am specifically thinking of the first version of his book which pertained to -- in which he made some comments which the Jewish community found highly offensive and which were removed in the subsequent publication of that book.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Removed by whom?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: By President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: So after he found that the Jewish community found them offensive, he had them removed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's correct, yes. He issued a revised version of the book which was actually a substantial revision.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: What does that indicate to you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: It indicates that my original statement that he -- your original proposition that there was no hatred expressed toward any group is not a valid statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Let's rewind. You, in Blaskic, of course, agreed that there was no hatred to any group expressed in his books?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I did not. I said that the version of the book that I had at hand was at issue, so I can't concur with your conclusion here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Fair enough. But I want to raise this issue of the reaction of Jewish folks who read the book. When, apparently, Dr. Tudjman heard about that, he changed the book; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: He reissued the book, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Okay. Can we also agree, in his writings, Dr. Tudjman does not specifically advocate a course or action in a particular situation. He isn't specific?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would agree, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I think we've already pointed out that the source hasn't been that Lord Owen noted that as of November 1992, Dr. Tudjman had accepted and recognised the borders of Bosnia would be -- well, I'm garbling that. Dr. Tudjman, as of this time, had accepted the recognition of BiH within its internationally recognised borders.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: There are a number of quotations that I took from Lord Owen, I believe, and that sounds right, but I can't specifically verify it for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, I note in your report to us, at page 34, that you note that Dr. Tudjman argued that Bosnia should be part of Croatia based on Croatia's economic and geopolitical interests and on the ethnic composition of Western Herzegovina and Central Bosnia. Now, do I take that to mean your work concluded, at least as to this section, that there was an economic union between the two areas?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't conclude that, no. There is an economic relationship, an important economic relationship between the two areas, and I think that in trying to characterise President Tudjman's understanding, he postulates the notion, and this is from his work published in, I think, 1981, the Columbia University book, press book, he spells out at some length his views on the geopolitical, economic whole that he believes constitutes what, to him, should be part of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And, indeed, that economic whole had been, prior to 1981, et cetera, the whole nation of Yugoslavia which benefited from being just that, a nation; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, and there were economic relations across those boundaries under the socialist republic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, you note at page 36 of your report the population from 1961 to 1991, and you cite the statistics there. Is it fair to say that the Croatian population was relatively stable during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: The Croatian population was relatively stable, and the Muslim population grew during that period of time, throughout the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina and most of the constituent parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The result, of course, is that the Croats became a smaller and smaller minority?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Depending on the area which one looks at, that is not true across the board. In some areas, the percentages actually remained quite stable. The Croatian emigration was, in fact, part of the -- there are a number of reasons for it, but this is not merely a matter of the number of people who were there staying stable but the -- go ahead. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Doctor, I just want to stick to a very small point, and that is, you show in your chart, Muslims and Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, 1961 to 1991, the nation as a whole, that is to say, Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Looking at the totality of that situation, the Croats were becoming a smaller and smaller minority?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: The word "minority" may not quite be appropriate here, since there was no majority group.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: But they were becoming a smaller percentage of the total population of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You were also asked, and I'm going to ask you again, whether or not your study in this area has concluded whether there were specific plans by Dr. Tudjman to expel people from Bosnia. Do you recall that discussion with Judge Riad?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think I interpreted his question as meaning, were there specific plans in terms of what to do with those people who were the targets of the expulsion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Let's go through that then. The question was: "JUDGE RIAD: Quoting Lord Owen's book, Balkan Odyssey, and mentioning Dr. Tudjman had one goal, 'to control the territory which he believed historically belonged to Croatia,' what was precisely the territory mentioned and were there any plans foreseen to gain this territory?" You answered something about a theoretical position, and the judge refined it, and he said: "JUDGE RIAD: Any steps to implement this wish ..." And the judge further went on to say: "... but as far as the population were concerned, were there any plans, as far as the people living in these areas, plans for people living in these areas? What were they supposed to be dealt with?" And then you asked: "A Oh, you mean the people who were not Croats?" He said yes, and your answer was: "A No. I know of no specific plans that were created to deal with the non-Croatian population, no. I don't think that there was. That wasn't something that was, let us say, premeditated, a preplanned part of these annexation ambitions." Do you recall your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You essentially told the judge, apparently under an interpretation you now give, that there were no plans by Dr. Tudjman relative to these folks; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. You may hear me, in that answer, trying to grasp exactly what he meant, and my answer pertained to were there plans in terms of what to do to dispose of the non-Croat population of these areas. That's the answer that I, at the time, intended to give him, and my answer today would be there were no plans that I know of that had been drawn up and drafted for the removal or disposition of the non-Croat population.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The reference --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me see if I've got this right. We don't have the transcript in front of us, so I don't know how this question arose, but as you recollect, Doctor, were you being asked about President Tudjman or about other plans?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think I was being -- as I recall, sir, I was being asked about President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It would be helpful to us if you could answer the question in relation -- give us your answer, yes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Let me suggest that I know of no plans that President Tudjman held, drew up, or promulgated which specifically provided for the expulsion or disposition of the non-Croat population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Perhaps, for the Court's edification, we can put first page 853 and then page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think this point has been clarified, unless anybody else wants to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: For the record, it's 853, 854, and 855 of the Blaskic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Doctor, let's see if we can also agree on a couple of principles. As a watershed, the dissolution of Yugoslavia as a nation was completed by April 27, 1992? Would you agree with that? That's the conclusion of the Badinter commission?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: As a state, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Although it's been said in this trial in a variety of places and ways, the Muslims were the most numerous nation within BiH, about 43 per cent?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And the Croats were the smallest, about 17 per cent?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And then there were 31 per cent Serbs, Yugoslavs, and others?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think the percentage of Yugoslavs was somewhere around five or six per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. I misread my own notes. There were 31 per cent Serbs, five per cent Yugoslavs, and two per cent others?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Would you agree that the Muslims perceived themselves as a nation only recently, that is, within the past 20 or 30 years?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would make this distinction in my answer: I think that they became and perceived themselves as a political community much before that and, in fact, probably in the 19th century and defined themselves as a nation within the past 35 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. As a sovereign nation then, you say that they started to see themselves within the past 35 years?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would not use the word "sovereign."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. Do you agree that they started, at one point in time, that is, the Muslims and BiH, to see themselves as a sovereign nation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: You do not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: The word "sovereign" and "nation" in this sense don't go together. I think that that terminology, if you're looking at the period from, say, the 1960s, enters into the assertions of the political rhetoric, but in terms of being sovereign, that is, not subject to the authority or jurisdiction of some other state, that would be an incorrect interpretation of the term. I just offer that as a clarification of what you're defining.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Certainly we can agree that the Muslims were the only peoples within Yugoslavia that couldn't point to one of the republics as their own republic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: They pointed to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina as their republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: They couldn't point like the Serbs to Serbia, the Croats to Croatia. They said, "This land is ours." That's your opinion, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, they pointed to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as the place in which most of them lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, maybe I'm confused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think you better slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I'm confused by your answer, Doctor. Did they see Bosnia-Herzegovina as their nation? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I did not say that, and that's not the formulation. Let me just perhaps suggest the formulation that was used, and that was that the Bosnian Muslims are a nation, starting in, let's say, sometime in the 1960s, and they live in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and, together with the nations of the Croats and Serbs, find this to be their homeland.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Indeed, Bosnia-Herzegovina was always known --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Pause for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Very good, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Excuse me, Mr. Stein. I should like to complete this information that is being given to us by the expert, Dr. Donia. You made a distinction in your report between Bosnian and Bosniak. Could you please clarify this distinction for us?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I'll try. In 1993, the Bosnian Muslim leadership met and decided to change the name of their group from the Bosnian Muslims to the Bosniaks. This was done principally because the Bosnian Muslim name no longer reflected the nature of the community because the Bosnian Muslim nation consisted of many people who were secular Muslims or even non-practising or atheistic Muslims. It sounds like a contradiction which is why the name change took place. Thus, from 1993 on, one finds the term "Bosniak" universally deployed by the international community to refer to the group previously called the Bosnian Muslims, and the same takes place for domestic use within Bosnia. Thus, the term "Bosniak" is distinct from Bosnian in that the term "Bosnian" refers to any person who is an inhabitant of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I will share with you my own assessment of that name change. It solved one problem, which was the religious association with the now secular nationality, but it created another one, which is the one that you've just raised, namely that the distinction between "Bosnian" and "Bosniak" requires subtlety and close attention to detail, both in foreign languages and in the language of the region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) To make this quite clear, I consider it to be very important and interesting, you said that the term "Bosnian Muslims" no longer reflected the reality of the community because there were people among them who were secularised. There were others who were even atheist. How could you qualify the religious practice within Bosnia in this period of time which you studied in your work and in your report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is perhaps ironic that just at the time that the name was changed, in fact, there was greater religious observance being practised, and that trend really began some time late in the socialist period, perhaps the 1980s, and continues to this day. The practising Muslims will now frequently describe themselves as Bosniak by nationality and Muslim by religion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: While we're on this subject, I'm given to understand and I ask your comment, Mr. Izetbegovic apparently does not prefer to use and is against the name "Bosniaks"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: There are a number of people who are opposed to the use of the term "Bosniak," and many of them are my colleagues as historians. Amongst the Bosnian Muslim community, some of them are, in fact, opposed to it because they are not Bosniaks or Bosnian Muslims and object to this very close similarity of terms. So I would say that there is broad consensus within the community of Bosnian Muslims -- that there is general agreement but far from complete consensus.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: On the use or non-use?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the term "Bosniak." It's regularly used in the press, it's universally used by the International Community to distinguish Bosnian Muslims from other nationalities, but within the group, the term as a term of self-ascription is not universally agreed upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Going back to where we were before we took an interesting discursive on the term "Bosniak," Bosnia was indeed referred to as the Republic of Croats, Serbs, and Muslims after World War II?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's exactly right. That formulation was carefully -- it's interesting to, say, look at the constitution of 1974 for Bosnia, which in the first three provisions lists the Muslims first in one, the Croats first in one, and the Serbian first in one. So there was this official effort to provide complete equality of recognition of these three nationalities within Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: It also seems like that is a recognition of the fact that there are three distinct nationalities within BiH as opposed to Slovenia, Serbia, Croatia, where there are certainly minority peoples but are known as the home of the Croats, the Serbs, or the Slovenes?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Again, I'm not a constitutional specialist on this, but I don't think that -- the socialist constitutions of those republics, I think they recognise the status of the other nationalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I understand that, but my point is, I guess, not a political or constitutional one, it's more of a nationalist one. In the loose sense of the word, BiH was also, as well as in the official sense, the home of the Croats, the Slovenes, and the Muslims, whereas the other republics were, with certain of the minorities, the home of the Croats?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I grant your nationalistic point and would note that Bosnia is, in fact, the only republic without a national majority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Excuse me, Dr. Donia. You're talking about an absolute majority or a relative majority?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No one had an absolute majority. No group had an absolute majority in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So I'm speaking of a relative majority or what I think of as a plurality which would have been that of the Bosniaks or Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Doctor, Mr. Izetbegovic is quoted as saying: "We want to have a state because a people without a state is a family that was expelled to a meadow. It rains and the family does not have a roof over its head. People without a state are as that family without a roof. God save us from belonging to the people without a state." I'm going to skip a few lines. "In our state, we will live how it suits us. No one will prescribe us how we should live as it was before the case. One thing is sure: In this state, Islam will be respected." Doctor, I want to ask you about that quote. Firstly, are you familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe it comes from the Islamic declaration written by Mr. Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: What do you take it to mean, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I take it to be one of the ambivalent statements that Mr. Izetbegovic and many others make regarding the status of the relationship between the Bosnian Muslims and the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Part of that quote, that is, the notion that the Bosnian Muslims must have a state, that is, a state which they call home, I think has been implemented in the period after the collapse of socialism and, in some sense, existed even before it, although I'm sure President Izetbegovic would not agree with that. The notion that we will do anything we want to in that state is a statement that I think he would not make himself today and not seek to implement. I don't mean by that to suggest that the Bosniak community will not exercise its power within Bosnia and Herzegovina within reasonable ways, but it will seek and pursue power, in other words, but it has not sought to willy-nilly disregard legal norms, conventions within Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: In 1994, Doctor, December, Mr. Izetbegovic is quoted as saying: "Finally, we are becoming a nation and we are creating our country. All nations did it in blood. History does not make gifts. We cannot be an exception." Doctor, I ask you, doesn't it seem to you, in 1999, looking back at this period, that Mr. Izetbegovic was, A, clearly indicating his goal for a Muslim state in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't concur.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: My second question along these lines, even though you don't agree with the first statement, would you agree that Mr. Izetbegovic certainly has, throughout his writings and his philosophy, indicated that he wanted to have an independent Muslim state in BiH?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Let's talk for a minute, if we can, about the SDA party. The SDA party is the Party of Democratic Action?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Stranka Demokratske Akcije, which is the Muslim party, which bears no name, Muslim or Bosniak, within it but is nevertheless the expression of that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: It was established in 1990, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: By the way, the SDS, which is the Serbian party, was established in July of 1990; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And the SDA in May of 1990?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And the HDZ in August of 1990?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: So the HDZ was the last of the parties established?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: At the time the SDA was established, would you agree it was actually established -- I know you're an historian and not a lawyer or constitutionalist -- would you agree it was established illegally?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was actually established at a time when it was unclear what the future legislation was going to be regarding the naming of the political formations that were then being brought together. This explains why the name "Muslim" or "Bosniak" does not appear within it because it was formed at this period of uncertainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The period of uncertainty is still Yugoslavia law is outstanding; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yugoslavia law is outstanding at that point in time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And that forbade the names of nationalistic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Stein, you're not bearing in mind the interpreters. Will somebody sit next to him and tell him?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I think that's the ultimate stroke, Judge. I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I was a tad thrown off, so I will try again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: It was illegal to use nationalistic names during this period of time, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: During the time that the SDA was formed, yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Can we agree that among the people who established the SDA, 40 of the real originators were from the Young Muslims -- I'm sorry, not 40, eight. Do you know what the Young Muslims are?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do, and I just don't know. The number sounds right. There was certainly some Young Muslim participation in the formation of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And the Young Muslims, sir, to familiarise the Court and everyone else, were what?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: The Young Muslims were a group that first organised in the 1930s and were associated with a specifically Islamic understanding of how society ought to be organised. They were subject to various imprisonment and persecution both by the inner war Yugoslavia state and by the socialist regime immediately after World War II and came to reconstitute themselves as Yugoslavia started to come apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Are you aware, sir, also in the election campaigns for the SDA, that the SDA used religious leaders to attract people to their party?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I'd say they did and all political formations did of the three nationalist groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: So all the three nationalist groups used their religious figures to gather the faithful, if you will?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: As of September 1990, can we agree that Mr. Izetbegovic announced that the SDA opposed the principle of a national parity and that the next government would be best formed on the basis of one man, one vote?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I couldn't either confirm that for you, nor certainly would not argue with the likelihood that he made that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. That's the same principle we hearkened to earlier in today's discussion, that is, the one man, one vote principle versus the one federation principle, which was discussed by Milosevic, if you recall.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't share -- I mean, you're leaping over many events in the meantime and in a very different context, so I don't know that I've stipulated that this is the instant principle in both cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. Doctor, according, again, to Ms. Silber and Mr. Little, they claim that: "Izetbegovic announced in 1990 that the SDA opposed the principle addition of a national parity and that the next government would be formed on the basis of one man, one vote. Izetbegovic was attempting to play the same game in Bosnia that Milosevic had in mind for Yugoslavia." That's where I got that concept.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I appreciate that there's a wealth of information in that volume, I use it myself very frequently, but I don't always find their conclusions and parallels to be ironclad in terms of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Right. Their point is that unless civil and individual rights were secured through institutions, majority vote would guarantee Serb domination throughout the country in the case of Mr. Milosevic. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And in Bosnia, the same principle would give the Muslims, the Republic's largest ethnic group, 44 per cent of the 4.35 million population, that is the greatest authority, one man, one vote?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. That's not the case and that's not the way that events evolved, which is my problem with that conclusion. Amongst the Muslim voters who went to the polls on November 18th, 1990, there was a substantial percentage who voted for non-nationalist parties. There were also some Croats who did so and a few Serbs, but the assumption, which was made by some nationalists in 1990, that every single person of Croat nationality would vote for the HDZ, that every single Muslim would vote for the SDA, proved to be -- or that every Serb would vote for the SDS, never came about and, in fact, until very late in the election campaign, the great fear of all three nationalist parties was, in fact, the triumph of the reform communists and socialists. They operated effectively as partners in the election campaign, so I don't -- I can't follow this -- I can't agree to this linearity between a one man, one vote, the principle, and the ultimate outcome for the communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Well, Doctor, let me make sure I understand. Certainly we can agree that during the elections that you just talked about, 83 per cent of the Croats voted for the HDZ, 78 per cent of the Serbs voted for the SDS, and 76 per cent of the Muslims voted for the SDA.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Those are --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Those are facts on which we can agree?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: So that the constituent peoples were, in fact, voting for these parties along constituent lines.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Largely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. The SDA was also established in Croatia, Serbia, Montenegro, Macedonia, Germany, Switzerland, America, and Canada, among others, would you agree?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Of course, President Izetbegovic was elected on 30 November, 1991, I have, but I think that may be actually 26 May, 1990?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think your May date is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: He was re-elected on 30 November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I think that -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The objectives of the SDA were the introduction of religious holidays, state holidays -- I'm sorry, introduction of religious holidays as a state holiday. That was one of the objectives? I'm sorry, Doctor, maybe -- can we agree that one of the objectives of the SDA was the introduction as a state holiday of religious holidays?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: One of many objectives, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Okay. And some of the others?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't have their platform in front of me and I couldn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, can we focus for just a minute, because we focused on certainly Dr. Tudjman, on Mr. Izetbegovic, the other party who was controlling some of the events in this region. It's reported from his early youth he dedicated himself to Islamic work. Is that fair, with your knowledge of Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, and I would say that I think he was in youth and remains a devout Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: He was part of the Young Muslims that we talked about earlier?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Very much so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: He was arrested in 1946, was he not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And his arrest was for significant participation in founding the Muslim journal Mud Zijad, M-u-d Z --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's the relevance of all this? 1946. Come on. Let's move closer to the events in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Mr. Izetbegovic also started writing, as did Dr. Tudjman; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: His first -- or his doctrine is set out in the Islamic declaration that you mentioned earlier?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by "doctrine."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Well, his feelings, his ideas, his thoughts are set out?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would say his general philosophy of history finds its expression in that work.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: That was first published in 1970?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, but I think it dates somewhat earlier, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And it was republished in 1990?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: He advocated, in the Islamic declaration, a general Islamic moral and religious regeneration; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can't stipulate to that without having some documentation to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Have you read the Islamic declaration?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: A return to true Islamic values? "Yes" or "No."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would say that's a fair summary of much of the declaration, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Re-Islamisation of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yeah, I think that's accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And the creation and strengthening of different types of Islamic unity?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And finally, struggling up to and including political and armed war for the creation of Islamic order in countries where Muslims represent majority or near majority of the population?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Without having the language in front of me, I couldn't stipulate to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Is that a fairly close characterisation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can't stipulate to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure what you mean by the term "stipulate." Could you agree or disagree that that's the essence of what he was saying?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Based on what I have in front of me and from my knowledge, I couldn't agree to that statement, no. That doesn't mean I would disagree with it upon closer inquiry but --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right. We'll take a look at it and provide it to you if we can, Doctor. Again, he was arrested in 1983; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: His arrests were for counter-revolutionary and conspiracy, and he was sentenced to 14 years in gaol?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the relevance of this, Mr. Stein? Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Sure. The OTP has decided, through this witness, to talk about Dr. Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. Why aren't you cross-examining about that instead of this, what seems to be a relevant matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The other player in the equation is of significance. The views expressed by the political leader of the Muslims in the SDA are significant in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But you're cross-examining him about his criminal record in 1983. Now, we need to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, let me ask you this: In the 1980 period and after his release from prison, Mr. Izetbegovic had rather extremist views about his nation and his people, will you agree?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: He aligned himself with Ayatollah Khomeini, "Yes" or "No?"

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say he aligned himself with Ayatollah Khomeini in any working since, no. He was very fond of being in touch with and travelling in the Islamic world, did so -- does so to this day, and has certainly courted the support of Islamic countries for Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And he's quoted in both 1984 and later in Belgrade in 1988 as saying: "There can be neither peace more coexistence between the Islamic faith and the non-Islamic social and political institutions." Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to order that you move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: All right, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And quickly, because we're going to adjourn soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Stein, you are at liberty to call an expert on Mr. Izetbegovic if you wish. You can do that through another expert, but this expert didn't come for that purpose. I think you must accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I must say we have had no particular evidence about Mr. Tudjman, so I'm not sure that I see any relevance about Mr. Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I take your point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's 5.27. I'm at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's only because I now find we aren't under the pressure of time that I'm not going to limit your cross-examination as I said earlier today, but you must have in mind the amount of time that's being taken about these matters. How much more have you got?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Whatever more I have is going to be cut and eliminated. I'll take a very close look at it, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Because we would want to start on the next witness tomorrow. Doctor, would you be back, please, at half past two tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I raise an administrative matter in relation to the next witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Stein is correct in say that we discussed the position he'd be facing in the version of the report in Serbo-Croat having been served the 10th of July, it seemed to me that if he was bound to be cross-examining beyond the end of week, then there would be no problem one way or another with his only having had the report in B/C/S whatever number of days it is, because Dr. Allcock can't come back next week in any event. Therefore, if there was outstanding cross-examination, it would have to be at a later date. Beyond that I hadn't gone into any agreement, and we'd simply left unresolved the question of entitlement of expert reports in B/C/S. But there's another administrative issue about Dr. Allcock and it is this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I wonder if we could let the witness go so he doesn't have to sit here listening to all of this. Thank you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We intend to introduce through Dr. Allcock a film, it lasts about an hour, that Your Honour, Judge May, has seen in the Kupreskic case, I think last week. It's called, "We're All Neighbours." It's by Tone Bringa. It would seem to me potentially possible to save Your Honour having to see that film a second time if we could effectively incorporate it in part of the pre-reading of the report, so that were Your Honour's two colleagues to have time and were we to have a copy of the film available either tomorrow morning or the morning after, or assuming that Your Honour's colleagues had the time, then they might be able to view that privately in the same way as the Defence will be able to do, and because Your Honour Judge May's recollection of the film will no doubt be very recent and alive, we could simply deal with the document as having been considered and cross-examination on it could take place directly. At the moment, I'm using the somewhat slow copying services here to ensure that there are copies of that video for the Defence tonight. Once that's done, I can then ensure that another copy is made available, or two, for the Judges Chambers should that be helpful. Alternatively, the original could be made available because it wouldn't be being used in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll see what arrangements have been made.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: We haven't seen the film. If it's appropriate and we view admissible, we will, I think, agree with my colleague. It seems a perfectly reasonable use of time if the technology exists to view it out of court, but I reserve until we see it to comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So far as this witness is concerned, Mr. Hart's (phoen) concerned, and I think rightly, that I should not let pass the issue whether it has to be formally produced as an exhibit in the case, that is, the report of Dr. Donia. I expect it does have to be produced and given a label but I'm not sure what the practice is in other cases. Can I leave that with the staff to deal with?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
